title: Savings, Spending and Budgeting Basics
subtitle: Take charge of your household money with a real monthly budget, an emergency fund and safe savings choices.
description: A practical, Nigeria-focused course on separating needs from wants, tracking income and expenses, saving safely, building an emergency fund and living on a monthly budget. You will also learn to judge loans by their real cost, spot loan scams and ponzi schemes, and teach children good money habits. This course explains options and risks; it is not personal financial advice.
outcomes: Sort household spending into needs and wants and track every naira for a month
Build and balance a written monthly budget, then adjust it in hard months
Set an emergency fund target and choose safe, licensed places to keep savings
Use ajo, esusu, adashe or a cooperative with written safeguards
Work out the true cost of a loan and recognise loan scams and ponzi schemes
Set SMART savings goals and teach children a save, spend and share habit
audience: Women managing household or small business money who want a clear, practical plan, whatever their level of schooling.
tools: A notebook and pen, or a phone notes or spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets
Your bank or mobile money app for transaction history
A calculator (the phone calculator is fine)

modules.title: Understanding Money and Your Financial Life
modules.overview: Start with a clear picture of your money. You will map your household finances, learn to separate needs from wants, and record your real income and expenses so every later decision rests on facts.

lessons.title: Your money map: the five money decisions every household makes
objectives: Name the five everyday money decisions: earn, spend, save, borrow and protect
Draw a simple money map of where your household money comes from and goes
Explain in plain words how rising prices (inflation) affect cash kept at home
Set one honest starting point for this course

blocks.text: Financial literacy simply means understanding money well enough to make good choices with it. It is not about being rich, having a degree or using big words. A market woman who knows exactly what each bag of rice cost her, what she sold it for and what she kept is practising financial literacy every day. This course builds on what you already do and gives you a few tools that make it easier.
Almost every money choice you make falls into one of **five decisions**. Learning to see them clearly is the first step.

head: Decision
The question it answers
Everyday Nigerian example
rows: Salary, sales from a shop, tailoring jobs, money sent by a husband or child
What do I pay for, and is it worth it?
Foodstuff, rent, school fees, transport, data
What do I keep for later?
A bank savings account, ajo contribution, money set aside for rent
When do I use someone else's money, and at what cost?
Loan from a cooperative, buying on credit from a supplier, a loan app
How do I keep my money and family safe from shocks and fraud?
An emergency fund, never sharing your BVN or OTP, avoiding "double your money" offers

blocks.name: personal-finance
blocks.alt: A woman reviewing money and charts
blocks.caption: Seeing your money clearly, in one place, is where good decisions start.

blocks.text: Draw your money map

A **money map** is a quick drawing of your household finances. Put a circle in the middle of a page and write "Our household". On the left, draw arrows coming in, one for each source of money. On the right, draw arrows going out, one for each big type of spending. At the bottom, draw a box for savings and a box for debts. You do not need exact figures yet. The goal is to see the whole picture on one page.

Many people discover two things the first time they do this. First, money comes from more places than they thought, such as small side sales or gifts. Second, a lot of money leaves through small, frequent spending that never felt important: daily transport, airtime, snacks for the children, small contributions at events.

blocks.title: How money moves through a household
items: Money comes in
Plan and spend
Save first portion
Repay any debt
Review each month
blocks.caption: Money should follow a plan from the moment it arrives, not only when it runs out.

blocks.text: Why cash under the mattress loses value

When prices of goods rise over time, economists call it **inflation**. If a paint of garri cost less last year than it does today, that is inflation at work. The important lesson is this: ₦10,000 kept in a tin at home is still ₦10,000 next year, but it buys less. Cash at home can also be stolen, burnt or eaten by rats, and it is easy to spend on impulse. That is why later in this course we compare safer places to keep savings.

blocks.title: Worked example: the same money, two choices
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells pepper soup and keeps her savings in a tin at home. Her neighbour Halima saves the same amount in a bank savings account.
steps: Both save about ₦5,000 every week for a year, which is about ₦260,000 (52 weeks x ₦5,000).
Twice during the year Ngozi takes from the tin for things that were not planned, such as a party outfit, and she does not put the money back. She ends the year with about ₦190,000.
Halima's money is not in front of her. It needs a transfer to spend, which gives her time to think. She ends with her full ₦260,000 plus a small amount of interest.
Both women face rising prices, so neither amount buys as much as it would have a year earlier.
blocks.result: The biggest difference was not interest. It was that Halima's money was harder to spend on impulse and safe from theft. Where you keep savings changes how much you keep.

blocks.text: Start where you are

You may feel behind, or ashamed of past money mistakes. Most people have made them. What matters is having a clear picture now and a simple plan. In this course you will build that plan step by step: knowing your needs and wants, tracking income and expenses, saving with purpose, making a monthly budget, and borrowing only when it makes sense.

blocks.title: This course is education, not advice
blocks.text: We explain options and their risks so you can decide for yourself. Your situation is unique. For big decisions, such as a large loan or investment, speak to a licensed professional and check that any company is registered with the right regulator.

items: Keep your money map somewhere private, such as a notebook you keep safe.
Include everyone who contributes to or depends on the household money.
Write today's date on it. You will compare it with a new map at the end of the course.

takeaways: Every money choice is one of five decisions: earn, spend, save, borrow or protect.
A one-page money map shows where money comes from and where it goes.
Inflation means the same naira buys less over time.
Where you keep savings affects how much you actually keep.

activity.title: Draw your first money map
steps: Take a clean page and write "Our household" in a circle in the middle.
Draw an arrow in for every source of money you receive in a normal month.
Draw an arrow out for every main type of spending, including small daily ones.
Add a savings box and a debts box at the bottom, with rough amounts if you know them.
Circle the one arrow out that surprises you most.
activity.evidence: A photo of your money map with today's date on it

lessons.title: Needs vs wants: deciding what comes first
objectives: Tell the difference between a need and a want using a simple test
Sort your own household spending into needs, wants and savings
Use a waiting rule to avoid impulse buying
Handle social pressure to spend at events and in the family

blocks.text: A **need** is something you must have to live safely, stay healthy and keep earning: basic food, safe shelter, clean water, essential healthcare, basic clothing, school fees for your children, and the transport or tools you need for work. A **want** is something that makes life nicer but you could live without, or delay, for now: a new phone when your old one works, aso ebi for every event, eating out, the latest shoes.

The line is not always simple, because many items have a need part and a want part. Food is a need, but rice and stew at home costs far less than buying food outside every day. Transport to work is a need, but a ride-hailing car when a bus would do is partly a want. Your phone may be a need for your business, but an expensive new model is a want.

blocks.name: choice
blocks.alt: A person choosing between two options
blocks.caption: Before you buy, pause and ask: is this a need, or a want I can delay?

blocks.text: The three-question test

items: Ask: what happens if I do not buy this today? If the answer is that my family goes hungry, falls sick, loses shelter or I cannot work, it is a need.
Ask: is there a cheaper version that meets the same need? The basic version is the need. The extra cost is the want.
Ask: can this wait 30 days? If it can wait, it is probably a want. Write it on a "wants list" instead of buying it now.

blocks.title: Need or want?
items: Needs
Wants
blocks.caption: Many items have a need part and a want part; the basic version is the need.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting one week of spending
blocks.context: For example, Aisha, a hairdresser in Kaduna, wrote down everything she spent in one week. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Foodstuff from the market: about ₦18,000. Need.
Bus fare to the salon: about ₦6,000. Need.
Hair products for clients: about ₦9,000. Need for work.
Suya and soft drinks three evenings: about ₦7,500. Want.
Contribution for a friend's aso ebi: about ₦15,000. Want.
Data and airtime: about ₦3,000. Partly need (business WhatsApp), partly want (video streaming).
Total about ₦58,500, of which about ₦22,500 was clearly wants.
blocks.result: Aisha did not cut every want. She kept one suya evening (about ₦2,500) and declined the aso ebi this time. That freed about ₦20,000 that week for her emergency savings.

blocks.text: Wants are not bad

This lesson is not about never enjoying anything. Wants give life joy, and cutting every one usually fails after a few weeks. The goal is to **pay for needs first, save next, and then enjoy wants with what is left**, knowingly. A small planned treat is better than a big unplanned one that leaves you short for rent.
The 30-day wants list

Impulse buying happens when we see something and buy it on the spot, often because of a sales pitch, a WhatsApp status or a friend's purchase. A simple defence is the **30-day wants list**. When you feel like buying a non-essential item, write it down with the price and the date. If you still want it after 30 days and you have the money without touching savings or needs, buy it. You will find that many items drop off the list on their own.

blocks.title: Handling social and family pressure
blocks.text: Weddings, burials, naming ceremonies and family requests are real parts of life. Decide in advance how much you can give each month for events and family support, and keep to it. It is fine to say: "I cannot buy the aso ebi this time, but I will come and celebrate with you." Giving within your plan protects your own children's needs.
Needs change with your situation

Shopping habits matter too. Go to the market with a written list and a set amount of cash or a set transfer limit. Buying staples such as rice, beans and oil in larger quantities, when you can afford to and can store them safely, often costs less per cup than buying small amounts daily. Some women share a bulk bag with a trusted neighbour and split the cost. Avoid shopping when you are hungry or rushed, because that is when wants slip into the basket.

A need for one family may be a want for another. A generator may be a need for a woman who runs a frozen food business, but a want for someone whose work does not depend on power. Be honest with yourself about your own situation, not what neighbours do. Review your needs list every few months, because children grow, rent changes and businesses change.

items: Needs keep you safe, healthy and earning.
Wants make life nicer but can be delayed or reduced.
Savings are treated like a need: paid early, not from leftovers.

takeaways: A need protects your life, health, shelter or ability to earn; a want can wait.
Many items have a basic need part and an extra want part.
Use the 30-day wants list to beat impulse buying.
Decide in advance how much you give to events and family support.

activity.title: Sort a week of spending
steps: Write down everything you spent in the past seven days, as best you can remember.
Mark each item N for need, W for want, or N/W if it is partly both.
Add up the W items and the want part of the N/W items.
Choose one want to reduce next week and write how much it will free.
Start a 30-day wants list on the last page of your notebook.
activity.evidence: Your sorted spending list with need and want totals

lessons.title: Understanding income: regular, irregular and side income
objectives: List all the sources of income in your household
Explain the difference between gross income and take-home income
Work out a safe monthly figure from irregular income
Record income in a simple notebook or phone note

blocks.text: **Income** is all the money that comes into your hands or your account. Before you can plan spending or saving, you need to know how much really comes in each month and when it arrives. In many Nigerian households income comes from several places, and some of it is irregular. That is normal, and you can still plan with it.

head: Type of income
Examples
How predictable
rows: Monthly pay from a school, hospital, company or government
Sales from a provisions shop, food business, tailoring, hairdressing
Selling maize, yam, cassava or livestock
Comes in large amounts at harvest
Money from a spouse, children abroad, family
Selling on WhatsApp, POS agent commission, weekend catering

blocks.name: money-received
blocks.alt: A person receiving money on a phone
blocks.caption: Write down every inflow, even small transfers, so your picture of income is complete.

blocks.text: Gross income and take-home income

If you earn a salary, your **gross income** is the full amount on your offer letter. Your **take-home** or net income is what reaches your account after deductions such as tax (PAYE), pension contribution and any loan repayments taken by your employer. Always plan with take-home income, because that is the money you can actually use.

For a business, the money you collect from customers is not all income for your family. Part of it must go back to buy stock and pay costs. Your real income is your **profit**: sales minus business costs. A common mistake is to spend sales money at home and then find there is nothing left to restock. Keep business money and household money separate, even if it is only two envelopes or two bank accounts.

blocks.title: From sales to take-home money
items: Total sales collected
Minus stock and costs
Profit
Pay yourself fixed amount
Rest stays in business
blocks.caption: Paying yourself a fixed amount from profit keeps the business alive and the home budget steady.

blocks.text: Planning with irregular income

When income changes month to month, plan with a **careful average**, not your best month. Look back at the last three to six months, write down what came in each month, and use the lowest month or the average of the lower months as your planning figure. In good months, the extra goes first to savings or to a buffer that tops up lean months.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding a safe monthly figure
blocks.context: For example, Funke runs a small food canteen in Ibadan. Her profit (after buying ingredients and paying her helper) over six months was approximately as follows.
steps: Total for six months: about ₦560,000. Average: about ₦93,000 per month (₦560,000 divided by 6).
Her lowest month was about ₦70,000.
She chooses ₦80,000 as her safe planning figure, between the lowest month and the average.
In any month she makes more than ₦80,000, she moves the extra into a separate savings account as a buffer.
blocks.result: Funke now budgets her home spending on about ₦80,000. In a weak month the buffer fills the gap, so rent and school fees are never in danger.

blocks.title: Pay yourself a salary from your business
blocks.text: If you run a business, choose a fixed amount to transfer to your personal account on the same day each week or month. This turns irregular sales into a steadier household income and protects your stock money.
Keeping an income record

Large one-off amounts need special care. A harvest payment, a gift from a child abroad, a contract payment or a bonus can feel like a lot of money, and requests often arrive the moment people hear about it. Before spending any of it, decide how much will cover the months ahead, how much goes to savings, and how much is truly free. A farmer who receives most of her year's income at harvest should divide it into monthly amounts so the family is not short in the planting season.

Use one page per month in a notebook, or a note on your phone. Write the date, the source and the amount every time money comes in. Bank and mobile money apps such as Opay, Moniepoint, PalmPay or your bank app show a transaction history, which helps, but cash income must be written down by hand or it disappears from your picture. At the end of the month, add it up.

items: Write the date, source and amount for every inflow.
Separate business sales from household income.
Add up totals at month end and note the lowest month.
Keep records private and safe, because they show your money details.

takeaways: Plan with take-home income, not gross salary.
Business income for the home is profit, not total sales.
With irregular income, plan with a careful average and save the extra in good months.
Write down cash income, because apps only show digital money.

activity.title: Build your income record
steps: List every source of money your household received in the last three months.
Write the amount for each month as accurately as you can.
Work out the average and note the lowest month.
Choose a safe monthly planning figure and write it at the top of your page.
If you run a business, decide on a fixed weekly or monthly amount to pay yourself.
activity.evidence: Your income page showing three months, the average and your planning figure

lessons.title: Understanding expenses: tracking where every naira goes
objectives: Sort expenses into fixed, variable and irregular
Track spending for 30 days using a notebook or phone
Spot small daily leaks that add up
Turn yearly costs into a monthly amount to set aside

blocks.text: **Expenses** are everything you spend money on. Most people know their big expenses, like rent and school fees, but are surprised by how much goes on small, frequent items. The only way to know is to **track**: write down every naira you spend for a full month. It sounds tiring, but even two weeks of honest tracking teaches you more than months of guessing.
Three kinds of expenses

head: Kind
What it means
Examples
rows: Same amount, same time, every month or term
Rent paid monthly, school bus fee, cooperative contribution, loan repayment
Needed every month, but the amount changes
Foodstuff, transport, electricity tokens, fuel, data
Do not come every month, but are certain to come
Annual rent, school fees each term, festive season, medical check-ups, phone repair

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.caption: Keep receipts or write each purchase down; small amounts are the ones we forget.

blocks.text: Irregular expenses cause the most stress, because they feel like emergencies even though we knew they were coming. Annual rent is the classic example. The fix is to divide each yearly cost by 12 and set that amount aside every month. We will do this in the worked example below.
How to track for 30 days

items: Choose your tool: a small notebook you carry, the notes app on your phone, or a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets.
Every time you spend, write the date, what you bought and the amount. Do it immediately, or at the end of each day at the latest.
Include cash, transfers, POS payments, airtime and data, and money given to others.
At the end of each week, group the spending into categories such as food, transport, utilities, children, business, giving and personal.
At the end of the month, add each category and compare it with what you expected.

blocks.title: The tracking habit
items: Spend
Write it down
Group weekly
Review monthly
Adjust plan
blocks.caption: Tracking is a cycle: each month's review makes next month's spending wiser.

blocks.text: Small leaks, big holes

A leak is a small, frequent cost that feels harmless. Common leaks include buying drinks and snacks daily, paying extra for small data bundles instead of a monthly plan, bank charges from many tiny transfers, and buying foodstuff in very small quantities at a higher unit price. One leak on its own seems minor. Multiplied by 30 days, it can be the cost of a term's school uniform.

blocks.title: Worked example: leaks and yearly costs
blocks.context: For example, Blessing, a teacher in Port Harcourt, tracked her spending for one month. Amounts are approximate.
steps: She found she spent about ₦800 a day on drinks and snacks at work. Over 22 working days that is about ₦17,600 a month.
She bought small daily data bundles costing about ₦8,000 in the month. A monthly plan with similar data would have cost noticeably less.
Her annual rent is about ₦480,000. Divided by 12, that is about ₦40,000 she should set aside every month.
Her children's school fees are about ₦90,000 per term, three terms a year: ₦270,000 a year, or about ₦22,500 a month.
blocks.result: By packing a drink from home on most days and switching to a monthly data plan, Blessing freed about ₦15,000 a month. Setting aside about ₦62,500 monthly for rent and fees means those payments no longer feel like emergencies.

blocks.title: Watch for unexplained debits
blocks.text: When you check your bank or mobile money history, look for charges you do not recognise, subscriptions you forgot, or transfers you did not make. Report any you did not authorise to your bank immediately through its official app, branch or customer care line, never through a number someone sends you.
What your tracking tells you

If writing every item feels too hard, try the **envelope count** instead. Start the week with a set amount of cash in an envelope for daily spending, and note how much is left each evening. For digital spending, open your bank or mobile money app every Sunday and read through the week's debits. Both methods show you the same truth: where the money actually went, compared with where you thought it went. Choose the method you will actually keep doing.

After a month, you will be able to answer three questions. How much do we spend on needs? How much leaks away on wants and small items? Which yearly costs do we need to save for monthly? These answers are the raw material for your budget in Module 3. Do not judge yourself harshly. The point is information, not guilt.

items: Track for at least two weeks, ideally a full month.
Include every channel: cash, transfer, POS, card, airtime.
Turn every yearly cost into a monthly amount by dividing by 12.
Fix one leak at a time rather than all at once.

takeaways: Expenses are fixed, variable or irregular.
Tracking every naira for a month is the fastest way to understand your spending.
Small daily leaks can add up to large monthly amounts.
Divide yearly costs by 12 and save that amount each month.

activity.title: Start a 30-day spending tracker
steps: Set up a page or phone note with columns for date, item, amount and category.
Record every expense from today, including cash and airtime.
List your yearly and termly costs and divide each by 12.
After the first week, circle your biggest leak.
Write one action to reduce that leak.
activity.evidence: Your first week of tracking plus your list of yearly costs divided by 12

quiz.q: Chioma keeps all her savings in a tin at home. Which risk is she most exposed to, besides theft?
options: Rising prices mean the money buys less over time, and it is easy to spend on impulse
Her savings will earn too much interest
The bank will charge her fees
Her savings will be taxed twice
quiz.explain: Cash at home earns nothing and loses buying power to inflation. It is also easy to dip into without thinking.

quiz.q: Which of these is best described as a want?
options: Paying the school fees for her children
Replacing a working phone with a newer model
Buying medicine prescribed for her son
Paying for bus fare to her shop
quiz.explain: A working phone already meets the need. The upgrade can be delayed, so it is a want.

quiz.q: Funke's canteen profit over four months was about ₦60,000, ₦90,000, ₦75,000 and ₦95,000. What is a careful monthly figure to plan her home budget with?
quiz.explain: With irregular income, plan near the lower months (average here is about ₦80,000; lowest ₦60,000). Extra in good months goes to savings or a buffer.

quiz.q: Annual rent is about ₦360,000. How much should be set aside each month to be ready when it is due?
quiz.explain: ₦360,000 divided by 12 months is ₦30,000 per month.

quiz.q: A trader collects ₦50,000 in sales in a day and spends it all at home. What mistake has she made?
options: She treated total sales as household income instead of profit, so she cannot restock
She should have kept it in cash
She should have spent it on wants
quiz.explain: Part of sales must go back into stock and costs. Only profit is available for the home.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an irregular but predictable expense?
quiz.explain: School fees come every term, not every month, but they are certain. Save for them monthly.

modules.title: Saving Money: Building Your Safety Net and Future
modules.overview: Learn why and how to save with purpose. You will set real goals, compare safe places to keep savings in Nigeria, use saving groups wisely, and build an emergency fund step by step.

lessons.title: Why save: goals, shocks and opportunities
objectives: Name the three main jobs savings do for a family
Set short, medium and long-term savings goals with amounts and dates
Explain the "pay yourself first" rule
Calculate how much to save each week to reach a goal

blocks.text: Saving means keeping part of today's money for tomorrow. It sounds simple, but when money is tight it can feel impossible. The secret is to give your savings a clear **job**. Money with a job is much easier to protect than money that is just "extra".
Savings do three main jobs:

items: **Protect** the family from shocks: illness, a job loss, a broken shop freezer, a sudden death in the family. This is your emergency fund, covered in Lesson 4.
**Reach goals** that cost more than one month's income: rent, school fees, a sewing machine, a deep freezer for a business, a plot of land.
**Seize opportunities**: buying stock in bulk at a good price, paying for a training course, starting a side business without borrowing.

blocks.name: savings
blocks.alt: A person putting coins into savings
blocks.caption: Give every naira you save a clear job, and it becomes much easier to protect.

blocks.text: Short, medium and long-term goals

head: Goal type
Time frame
Examples
rows: Emergency fund starter, next term's school fees, Christmas costs
Two years' rent, a business machine, a used car for transport business
Building a house, children's university fees, money for old age

blocks.text: A good savings goal is **specific**. "I want to save money" is a wish. "I will save ₦150,000 for a new industrial sewing machine by 31 March" is a goal. It has an amount, a purpose and a date, so you can work out the weekly or monthly saving needed.

blocks.title: Order of savings priorities
items: Starter emergency fund
Known upcoming costs
Business and life goals
Long-term future
blocks.caption: Build from the base: a small emergency fund first, then known costs, then bigger goals.

blocks.text: Pay yourself first

Most people save whatever is left at the end of the month. Usually, nothing is left. **Pay yourself first** turns this around: the moment money comes in, move your savings amount out before you spend on anything else. Treat savings like a bill you must pay. Even a small fixed amount, saved first and every time, beats a large amount you only hope to save.

Many banks and mobile money apps let you set an **automatic transfer** or a locked target savings plan on a fixed date. If your salary arrives on the 25th, set the transfer for the 25th. You never see the money in your spending account, so you do not miss it.

blocks.title: Worked example: working backwards from a goal
blocks.context: For example, Kemi sells provisions in Abeokuta and wants a deep freezer to add frozen chicken and fish to her shop. The freezer costs about ₦300,000 (approximate, prices change).
steps: She sets a date 10 months away.
₦300,000 divided by 10 months is about ₦30,000 a month.
That is about ₦7,000 a week (₦30,000 divided by about 4.3 weeks).
She already saves ₦3,000 a week, so she needs about ₦4,000 more each week.
From her tracking, she cuts daily take-away lunch (about ₦2,500 a week) and buys her shop stock in larger, cheaper quantities (about ₦1,500 a week saved).
blocks.result: Kemi now saves about ₦7,000 a week into a locked target savings plan. She also checks the freezer price again before buying, because prices may rise during the 10 months.

blocks.title: Plan for rising prices
blocks.text: If your goal is many months away, the price may go up before you buy. Add a margin (for example 10 to 20 percent) to the target, or check the price every few months and adjust your weekly saving.
Small amounts really add up

Do not wait until you can save a big amount. Saving ₦500 a day is about ₦15,000 a month and about ₦180,000 in a year. Starting small builds the habit, and the habit is what matters most. When income rises, increase the amount. A good rule is to save part of every increase: if your pay or profit goes up by ₦10,000, save at least half of that rise before lifestyle swallows it.

If you are paid daily, as many traders and artisans are, save daily too. Put a fixed amount aside at the end of each working day before counting what is left for home. A small locked box kept away from the shop, emptied into the bank every week, works well for cash businesses.

Saving also changes how you feel. Women who have even a small amount set aside often describe more peace of mind and more confidence when talking with family about money. Savings give you choices: you can say no to a bad loan, or say yes to a good opportunity.

items: Give every savings pot a name, an amount and a date.
Save first, spend after.
Use automatic transfers where you can.
Start small and increase as income grows.

takeaways: Savings protect, reach goals and seize opportunities.
A real goal has an amount, a purpose and a date.
Pay yourself first, ideally by automatic transfer.
Divide the goal by the number of weeks to know your weekly target.

activity.title: Set three savings goals
steps: Write one short-term, one medium-term and one long-term goal.
Give each an amount (approximate) and a target date.
Work out the monthly and weekly saving needed for the short-term goal.
Decide the day you will move that amount each week or month.
Write the goal on a card and keep it where you will see it.
activity.evidence: Your goal card showing amounts, dates and weekly targets

lessons.title: Where to keep savings in Nigeria: options and their risks
objectives: Compare bank savings accounts, microfinance banks, fixed deposits, app savings and government savings bonds
Check whether a bank or app is properly licensed before using it
Match each savings goal to a suitable place
Recognise warning signs of unsafe savings offers

blocks.text: Once you decide to save, the next question is **where**. The best place depends on the job of the money: how soon you might need it, how safe it must be, and whether earning interest matters. No single option is best for everyone. Below are the main formal choices in Nigeria, with honest pros and cons. Interest rates change often, so always check current rates directly with the provider.

head: Option
Good for
Main advantages
Main risks or limits
rows: Licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN); deposits insured by NDIC up to a limit; easy access
Interest is usually low and may not keep up with inflation; easy to withdraw on impulse
Small traders, people far from big bank branches
Licensed by CBN; often closer to markets; may collect from your shop
Check the licence carefully; NDIC cover for microfinance banks has its own limit

Usually higher interest than a savings account

blocks.name: bank
blocks.caption: Formal banks are licensed and supervised, which protects your savings in ways a tin at home cannot.

blocks.text: What NDIC deposit insurance means

The **Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)** protects depositors if a licensed bank fails. If your bank collapses, NDIC pays insured depositors back up to a set maximum per depositor per bank. The limit is different for commercial banks and for microfinance banks, and it has been changed over the years, so check the current figure on the NDIC website before relying on it. Money in an unlicensed scheme has **no** NDIC protection.
How to check a bank or app is genuine

items: Find the full registered name of the bank or company, not just the app name.
Check the CBN website for its list of licensed banks and other financial institutions.
For apps, read the "About" page: genuine ones name their licence or the licensed bank that holds your money.
If a platform promises investment returns, check that it is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Nigeria.
Search the company name with words like "scam" or "complaint" and read what real customers report.

blocks.title: Before you save anywhere
items: Licensed by CBN?
Insured by NDIC?
Clear withdrawal rules?
Realistic interest rate?
Real address and helpline?
blocks.caption: If any answer is no or unclear, do not put your savings there.

blocks.title: Worked example: matching goals to places
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano earns about ₦120,000 a month from her tailoring business. She has three savings jobs.
steps: Emergency fund, target about ₦150,000: she uses a separate savings account at a licensed commercial bank, with no debit card linked, so the money is safe but reachable within a day.
Shop rent of about ₦240,000 due in 12 months: she sets up a locked target savings plan in her bank's app, saving about ₦20,000 a month automatically.
Money for her daughter's secondary school fees in three years: once her emergency fund is full, she asks a DMO-listed stockbroker about the FGN Savings Bond and compares it with a fixed deposit.
blocks.result: Each pot has a place that suits its job: quick access for emergencies, a lock for rent, and a longer-term option for school fees.

blocks.title: Red flags for savings offers
blocks.text: Be very careful with anyone promising unusually high, guaranteed returns, paying you to bring in new members, asking you to pay into a personal account, or pressuring you to act fast. These are classic signs of a ponzi scheme, which we cover in Module 4. Licensed banks do not ask for your PIN, password or OTP.
Keep savings separate from spending

Whatever option you choose, keep savings in a **different account** from the one you spend from. Many people open a second account at the same bank and do not request a debit card for it. This small barrier gives you time to think before withdrawing. If you use a mobile money wallet for daily spending, keep only spending money there and move savings out.

Remember that interest is only part of the story. A higher rate means nothing if the provider is not genuine, or if the rules make it impossible to get your money in a real emergency. **Safety first, access second, returns third** is a sensible order for most beginners.

items: Emergency money: safe and quick to reach.
Known costs within a year: locked target savings.
Longer-term money: options with higher returns but less access, after the emergency fund is in place.

takeaways: Choose where to save by the job of the money: safety, access, then returns.
Licensed banks are supervised by the CBN and covered by NDIC up to a limit.
Always check licences before using a bank, app or investment platform.
Keep savings in a separate account from daily spending.

For each, decide how quickly you might need the money.
Choose a suitable option from the table for each goal.
Check the licence of the bank or app you plan to use and write down where you checked.

lessons.title: Ajo, esusu, adashe and cooperatives: saving with others safely
objectives: Explain how a rotating savings group and a daily collector work
Identify the main risks of informal saving groups
Set up written rules that make a group safer
Compare informal groups with registered cooperative societies

blocks.text: Long before banks reached every town, Nigerian women saved together. The Yoruba call it **ajo** or **esusu**, in the north it is often **adashe**, and the Igbo have **isusu**. These groups work because members trust each other and the regular contribution creates discipline. They remain popular because they are simple, local and require no paperwork. But they also carry real risks, so it is worth understanding them well.
How a rotating group works

In a **rotating savings group**, a fixed number of members each contribute the same amount at each meeting. At every round, one member collects the whole pot. The rotation continues until everyone has collected once. Nobody earns interest, but each member receives a large lump sum at some point, which is hard to get by saving alone.

blocks.title: A five-member rotating group
items: All contribute monthly
Member 1 collects
Member 2 collects
Members 3 to 5 follow
Cycle ends or restarts
blocks.caption: Everyone pays every round and collects exactly once.

blocks.title: Worked example: a monthly ajo
blocks.context: For example, ten market women in Ibadan agree to contribute about ₦20,000 each month for ten months.
steps: Each month the pot is ₦20,000 x 10 = about ₦200,000.
The order of collection is decided by drawing numbers at the first meeting and written in the record book.
Bisi draws number 2 and collects about ₦200,000 in month 2. She uses it to buy fabric stock in bulk.
Bisi must keep paying ₦20,000 every month until month 10, even though she has already collected.
Over ten months, every member pays in ₦200,000 and receives ₦200,000.
blocks.result: Early collectors get an interest-free advance; late collectors are effectively saving. The system only works if everyone keeps paying after collecting.

blocks.text: The daily collector

Another common type is the **daily or weekly collector**, often called an alajo or esusu collector. Traders pay a small amount each day, and the collector returns the total at the end of the month. In many arrangements the collector keeps one day's contribution each month as a fee. For example, if you contribute ₦1,000 a day for 31 days, you might receive ₦30,000 back. Ask about the fee clearly before you start.
The real risks

items: **The collector disappears** with members' money. There is usually no insurance and recovering the money is difficult.
**A member stops paying after collecting.** Later members then receive less or nothing.
**Loss to theft or fire** when cash is kept at home.
**Poor records**, leading to disputes about who paid what.
**No interest**, so inflation reduces the value of money saved for many months.

blocks.title: Protect yourself in any saving group
blocks.text: Join only groups of people you know well and can find. Never join a group that promises more than members put in, or one where you must recruit others to get paid; that is a ponzi scheme, not ajo.
Rules that make a group safer

items: Write the rules down: amount, dates, order of collection, penalty for late payment, and what happens if someone leaves.
Keep a record book signed at every meeting, or a shared spreadsheet, showing every payment.
Choose a treasurer and a second person to check the records together.
Where possible, keep group money in a group bank account that needs two signatories, not in one person's house.
Put long-standing, trusted members early in the rotation only if the group agrees, and ask early collectors for a guarantor.

blocks.text: Cooperative societies: the more formal step

A **cooperative society** is a member-owned group, such as a staff cooperative or a market traders' cooperative, that can be registered with the cooperative department of your state government. Registered cooperatives have bylaws, elected officers, accounts that can be audited, and often offer members savings plus loans at agreed rates. Registration does not remove all risk, so attend meetings, read the annual accounts and ask questions.

head: Feature
Informal ajo or adashe
Registered cooperative
rows: May pay dividends and charge interest on loans
Often available to members by agreed rules
Bylaws, audits and the state regulator give some recourse

blocks.name: team-collaboration
blocks.alt: A group of people working together
blocks.caption: Saving with others works best with written rules, clear records and trusted members.

blocks.text: Many women use both: a bank account for the emergency fund, and an ajo or cooperative for a specific lump-sum goal. That spreads the risk so that one problem does not wipe out everything.

Before you join any group, ask four questions. Who holds the money between meetings? Where are the records kept, and can I see them? What happened the last time a member could not pay? How long has the group been running? Clear, confident answers are a good sign. Vague answers, or pressure to join quickly, are a reason to wait.

takeaways: Rotating groups give each member one lump sum; nobody earns interest.
The biggest risks are a collector disappearing and members stopping after collecting.
Written rules, signed records and a two-signatory account make groups safer.
Registered cooperatives offer more structure but still need active members.

lessons.title: Building an emergency fund step by step
objectives: Explain what counts as an emergency and what does not
Calculate a starter target and a full target for your emergency fund
Choose a safe, reachable place to keep it
Plan how to rebuild the fund after using it

blocks.text: An **emergency fund** is money kept aside only for real, unexpected problems. It is the first and most important savings pot, because without it every surprise becomes a crisis, and crises push families into expensive loans, selling assets cheaply, or pulling children out of school.
What is an emergency?

blocks.title: Emergency or not?
items: Real emergency
Not an emergency
blocks.caption: If you knew it was coming, it belongs in a planned savings pot, not the emergency fund.
left: Loss of job or main customer

blocks.text: Known costs, such as rent and school fees, should have their own savings pots (Module 1, Lesson 4). Keeping them separate protects the emergency fund for true surprises.
How much do you need?

A common guideline from personal finance educators is to aim for **three to six months of essential expenses**. Essential expenses are the needs from your tracking: food, rent share, transport to work, utilities, school costs and medicine. If your income is irregular, or you are the only earner, lean towards the higher end.

That full amount can feel very large, so break it into stages. First save a **starter fund**, for example one month of essentials or a fixed amount you can reach in a few months. Then keep building towards three months, and later six.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting the target
blocks.context: For example, Amaka is a single mother in Enugu. From her tracking, her essential monthly expenses are approximately as follows.
steps: Food about ₦60,000, rent share about ₦25,000, transport about ₦15,000, electricity and water about ₦10,000, children's school costs about ₦15,000, medicine and toiletries about ₦5,000.
Total essentials: about ₦130,000 per month.
Starter target (one month): about ₦130,000.
Full target (three months): about ₦390,000. Long-term (six months): about ₦780,000.
She saves about ₦15,000 a month. The starter fund will take about 9 months; she adds any extra income to speed it up.
blocks.result: Amaka now has clear milestones. Each one makes her family safer, even before she reaches the full target.

blocks.name: shield
blocks.caption: An emergency fund shields your family's plans when something unexpected happens.

blocks.text: Where to keep it

Emergency money must be **safe** and **reachable within a day or two**, but not so easy to reach that you spend it on everyday things. A separate savings account at a licensed bank, without a debit card attached, is a common choice. Avoid locking it in a plan you cannot break, and never put it in investments that can lose value or in an informal scheme.

blocks.title: Make it harder to touch
blocks.text: Give the account a name in your banking app such as "Emergency only". Some women ask a trusted person to be the one who reminds them of the rule before any withdrawal.
Finding the money to start

If you feel there is nothing left to save, look back at your tracking from Module 1. Most families can find a starting amount from three places. First, one or two leaks, such as daily snacks or small data bundles. Second, a one-off amount, such as part of a bonus, a gift or a good sales week, which can give the fund a quick head start. Third, a small side income, such as selling items you no longer use. Even ₦2,000 a week is about ₦104,000 in a year.

Family pressure is a real threat to emergency funds. Relatives may ask for help with costs that are not true emergencies. You can still help within your giving budget, while keeping the emergency fund for your own household's shocks. It can help to keep the balance private.
Using it and rebuilding it

items: When an emergency happens, pause and confirm it is truly unplanned and necessary.
Take only what you need, and keep the receipt or a note.
Write down how much you took out.
Restart saving the next month, and temporarily put extra towards rebuilding the fund before other goals.

blocks.text: Using the fund is not failure. It is exactly what it is for. The only mistake is not rebuilding it. Many families also discover, after the first emergency, that they need a bigger fund than they thought, which is useful information.

Some emergencies can be reduced before they happen. Basic health insurance, such as a state health insurance scheme or an employer plan, can lower hospital costs. Keeping copies of important documents, keeping your phone protected and servicing equipment you depend on for work all make shocks smaller. Ask what is available in your state and what it really covers before you pay.

takeaways: The emergency fund is only for unplanned, necessary costs.
Aim first for a starter fund, then three to six months of essential expenses.
Keep it safe, separate and reachable within a day or two.
After using it, rebuild it before other goals.
