modules.title: Budgeting: Planning Your Money Month by Month
modules.overview: Turn your money picture into a plan. You will choose a budgeting method, build a full monthly budget, live on it with simple weekly habits, and adjust it calmly when income falls or prices rise.

lessons.title: What a budget is and three simple ways to make one
objectives: Explain a budget as a plan made before the month begins
Describe the 50/30/20 guideline and when to adapt it
Describe zero-based budgeting and envelope budgeting
Choose the budgeting method that fits your income and habits

blocks.text: A **budget** is a plan for your money, made **before** you spend it. It says: this month, this much is coming in, and this is exactly where it will go. Tracking (Module 1) looks back at what happened. A budget looks forward and tells your money what to do. Together they form a loop: plan, spend, track, compare, improve.

A budget is not a punishment or a sign that you are poor. Businesses, governments and wealthy families all use budgets. It simply means you decide in advance, calmly, instead of deciding under pressure at the market or when a relative calls.

blocks.name: budgeting
blocks.alt: A person planning a budget with charts
blocks.caption: A budget is a calm plan made before the month starts, not a list of regrets afterwards.

blocks.text: Method 1: the 50/30/20 guideline

A popular starting point divides take-home income into three parts: about **50 percent for needs**, **30 percent for wants**, and **20 percent for savings and extra debt repayment**. It is easy to remember and gives a quick check on whether spending is balanced.

It is a guideline, not a law. For many Nigerian households, especially where food and rent take a large share of income, needs may be 60, 70 or even 80 percent. That is not failure. The adjusted version might be 70 percent needs, 10 percent wants and 20 percent savings, or 75, 15 and 10 to start. The key idea is to protect a **fixed share for savings** and to keep wants limited and planned.

blocks.title: Classic guideline vs a tighter month
items: Classic 50/30/20
Adapted 70/10/20
blocks.caption: Adjust the shares to your reality, but always protect a share for savings.

blocks.text: Method 2: zero-based budget

In a **zero-based budget**, you give every naira a job until income minus planned spending and saving equals zero. Zero does not mean you spend everything; savings is one of the jobs. This method is very clear and works well for people who like detail and have a fairly steady income.
Method 3: envelopes or pots

The **envelope method** puts money for each category into its own envelope (for cash) or its own pot or sub-account (for digital money). When the food envelope is empty, food spending stops until next month, or you move money from a want envelope. Many bank and mobile money apps now let you create named savings pots, which works the same way.

head: Method
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Needs may be more than 50 percent; adjust honestly
Steady income, people who like detail
Cash users, people who overspend easily
Cash at home must be kept safe; do not carry all envelopes

blocks.title: Worked example: 50/30/20 in naira
blocks.context: For example, Zainab, a nurse in Abuja, takes home about ₦250,000 a month after deductions.
steps: Classic split: needs ₦125,000 (50 percent), wants ₦75,000 (30 percent), savings ₦50,000 (20 percent).
From her tracking, her needs (rent share, food, transport, utilities, her mother's medicine) are actually about ₦175,000, which is 70 percent.
She adapts: needs ₦175,000 (70 percent), wants ₦25,000 (10 percent), savings ₦50,000 (20 percent).
She moves the ₦50,000 to savings on payday, then lives on ₦200,000.
blocks.result: Zainab keeps her 20 percent savings by trimming wants, rather than pretending her needs are smaller than they are.

blocks.text: Budgeting with irregular income

If your income changes from month to month, budget with your safe planning figure from Module 1, not your hope. Some traders budget week by week instead of month by month: each Friday they count the week's profit, move savings first, set aside the weekly share of rent and fees, and then plan the coming week's food and transport. Any money above the plan goes to the buffer that protects lean weeks. The method is the same; only the time period changes.

Another approach for irregular earners is to rank budget lines in order and fund them one by one as money arrives: first savings and food, then rent savings, then transport, then the rest. In a weak month, the lines at the bottom wait. In a strong month, every line is funded and the extra tops up the buffer.

blocks.title: Pick one method and try it for three months
blocks.text: Every method works if you use it. Choose the one that feels most natural, try it for three months, then adjust. Many women combine them: an adapted 50/30/20 to set the shares, and envelopes or pots to stick to them.

Whatever method you choose, write your budget down. A budget kept only in your head is easily forgotten when pressure comes. A page in your notebook or a simple phone spreadsheet is enough. In the next lesson you will build your first full monthly budget, line by line.

takeaways: A budget is a forward plan; tracking looks back.
50/30/20 is a guideline; adapt the shares but protect savings.
Zero-based budgets give every naira a job, including savings.
Envelopes or app pots make limits visible and easy to keep.

activity.title: Choose your budgeting method
steps: Write your monthly take-home income (or safe planning figure).
Calculate the classic 50/30/20 split in naira.
Compare it with your real needs from your tracking.
Write your adapted percentages.
Choose one method (adapted 50/30/20, zero-based or envelopes) and note why.
activity.evidence: A note with your income, your adapted percentages and the method you chose

lessons.title: Building your first monthly budget line by line
objectives: List budget categories that fit your household
Fill in a monthly budget using your income and tracking
Include savings and yearly costs as monthly lines
Balance the budget so planned spending does not exceed income

blocks.text: Now you will build a real monthly budget. You need three things from earlier lessons: your monthly take-home income or safe planning figure (Module 1, Lesson 3), your tracked spending (Module 1, Lesson 4), and your savings goals with monthly amounts (Module 2). Set aside 30 to 45 minutes in a quiet moment.
Eight steps to your first budget

items: Write your total expected income for the month at the top. Use take-home pay, or the safe figure for irregular income.
Write your savings line first: emergency fund and goal savings. This is paying yourself first.
Add fixed needs: rent or monthly rent savings, school fees savings, loan repayments, cooperative contributions.
Add variable needs, using your tracking as a guide: food, transport, electricity, water, cooking gas, data, toiletries, medicine.
Add a giving line: church or mosque, family support, events. Choose a realistic, fixed amount.
Add wants: personal spending, outings, treats. Keep this modest but not zero.
Add a small buffer of about 5 percent for things you forgot.
Add everything up. If the total is more than income, reduce wants first, then variable needs, until it balances.

blocks.title: Order for filling your budget
items: Income
Savings first
Fixed needs
Variable needs
Giving and wants
blocks.caption: Fill from the top: savings and needs are protected before wants.

blocks.title: Worked example: a family budget in Lagos
blocks.context: For example, Tolu and her husband together take home about ₦400,000 a month. They have two children in primary school. All amounts are approximate.
steps: Savings: emergency fund ₦30,000; children's fees savings ₦30,000. Subtotal ₦60,000.
Fixed needs: rent savings (annual rent about ₦1,200,000 divided by 12) ₦100,000; cooperative contribution ₦10,000. Subtotal ₦110,000.
Variable needs: food ₦110,000; transport ₦35,000; electricity and water ₦15,000; cooking gas ₦8,000; data and airtime ₦8,000; toiletries and medicine ₦10,000. Subtotal ₦186,000.
Giving: church and family support ₦20,000.
Wants: family outing and personal spending ₦14,000.
Buffer: ₦10,000.
blocks.result: The budget balances exactly. Savings and rent are protected first, and wants get what is realistically left.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.caption: Add every line carefully; a budget only works if the total fits inside your income.

blocks.text: When the numbers do not balance

If your planned spending is higher than your income, you have three choices: spend less, earn more, or both. Start with wants. Then look at variable needs for cheaper options: cooking at home more, buying staples in bulk, walking short distances, choosing a cheaper data plan. If it still does not balance, the gap is telling you something important: income may need to rise, through extra hours, a side business or better pricing in your trade. Do not balance a budget by borrowing for everyday needs; that only moves the problem to next month with interest added.

Look closely at the food line in Tolu's budget. It is the biggest variable need, so small changes there make a big difference. Planning a weekly menu, buying staples such as rice, beans, garri and oil in larger quantities when cash allows, and cooking larger pots that last two days can reduce it noticeably without eating less. The same thinking applies to transport: combining errands into one trip saves fares every week.

Notice also that rent appears as a monthly line even though the landlord is paid once a year. This is the most important habit in the whole budget. The money moves every month into a separate rent pot, so when the rent date comes, the full amount is already waiting.

blocks.title: Couples and shared households
blocks.text: If you share money with a spouse or family, build the budget together where possible. Agree who pays which lines and how savings will be held. Clear agreements prevent misunderstandings and help everyone pull in the same direction.
Keep it simple

Your first budget does not need to be perfect. Use round numbers. Ten to twelve categories are enough. The first month will show you where your guesses were wrong, and that is how you improve. A simple paper budget that you look at every week is far more useful than a detailed spreadsheet you never open.

If you prefer a phone, a free spreadsheet app like Google Sheets lets you set up columns for category, planned and actual, with a formula to subtract one from the other. If you prefer paper, rule a page into the same three columns. Either way, keep it somewhere you will see it every week.

takeaways: Start with income, then savings, then needs, then giving and wants.
Turn yearly costs like rent into monthly lines.
Add a small buffer for forgotten costs.
If it does not balance, cut wants first, then trim needs, then look at income.

activity.title: Write your first monthly budget
steps: Write your expected income at the top of a page.
List savings lines first, then fixed needs, variable needs, giving, wants and a buffer.
Fill in amounts using your tracking and goals.
Add it up and adjust until the total equals your income.
Calculate the percentage share of savings and needs.
activity.evidence: Your completed one-page monthly budget that balances

lessons.title: Living on your budget: daily habits that make it work
objectives: Use envelopes, pots or a separate account to control spending
Run a 10-minute weekly budget check
Compare planned and actual spending and explain the difference
Respond to requests for money without breaking the plan

blocks.text: Writing a budget takes an hour. Living on it takes a month of small decisions. This lesson gives you habits that make those decisions easier. The idea is to build systems so that you do not have to rely only on willpower.
Set up your money system on payday

items: On the day income arrives, move savings to the savings account or pot first.
Move monthly rent savings and school fees savings into their own pots.
Pay fixed bills that are due: cooperative, loan repayments, subscriptions you need.
Divide food and transport money into weekly amounts, for example in four envelopes or by transferring a weekly amount to your spending wallet.
What remains in the spending account is for the other variable needs, giving and wants.

blocks.name: wallet
blocks.caption: Divide money into weekly amounts so you can see what is left at any moment.

blocks.text: Weekly amounts are powerful. If food money for the month is ₦80,000, giving yourself about ₦20,000 each week makes it obvious when you are overspending in week one, while there is still time to adjust.
The 10-minute weekly check

Choose one time each week, for example Sunday evening. Open your notebook or spreadsheet and your bank and mobile money apps. Write actual spending next to each planned line. Ask: am I on track? If a line is running high, decide now how to bring it back: spend less in that line next week or move money from a want.

blocks.title: The weekly budget loop
items: Plan the week
Spend from envelopes
Record actual spending
Compare with plan
Adjust next week
blocks.caption: A short weekly loop catches problems while there is still time to fix them.

blocks.title: Worked example: planned vs actual
blocks.context: For example, Ese in Benin City reviews her budget after week two. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Food: planned ₦40,000 for two weeks, actual ₦46,000. Over by ₦6,000 because she bought food for visitors.
Transport: planned ₦15,000, actual ₦12,000. Under by ₦3,000.
Wants: planned ₦10,000, actual ₦4,000. Under by ₦6,000.
She moves ₦3,000 from transport and ₦3,000 from wants to cover the food overspend.
Savings remain untouched at the planned ₦25,000.
blocks.result: By checking at mid-month, Ese fixed a ₦6,000 overspend without touching savings or borrowing.

blocks.text: Notice that Ese did not wait for the end of the month. A mid-month check gave her time to move money between lines. Moving money from one line to another is allowed; that is what a living budget does. The two rules are: never move money out of savings for a non-emergency, and always write the change down so the plan stays honest.

If one line is over plan every single month, the plan is wrong, not you. Increase that line in next month's budget and reduce another line to keep the total balanced. After two or three months, your budget will reflect how your household really lives.
When someone asks for money

Requests from relatives, friends and neighbours are part of life. A clear **giving line** in your budget lets you respond calmly. When a request comes, check what is left in the giving line. If there is enough, give gladly. If not, you can offer a smaller amount, offer help in another form, or say kindly that you cannot this month. Taking from savings or rent money for non-emergencies is how many families fall behind.

blocks.title: Protect your digital money
blocks.text: Check your account balance before you spend, so you are never surprised. Turn on transaction alerts. Never share your PIN, password, OTP or BVN with anyone, including someone who says they are from your bank. Real banks do not ask for these by phone, SMS or WhatsApp.

Requests often come with urgency: "please, I need it today". Urgency is not the same as emergency. It is fine to say you will check your budget and reply in the evening. That short pause helps you decide calmly, and it protects you from scams that use urgent messages, sometimes from hacked accounts of friends, to rush people into sending money.
Small habits that help

items: Shop with a list and a set amount.
Leave the debit card linked to savings at home, or do not request one.
Wait 24 hours before any unplanned purchase above an amount you choose, such as ₦10,000.
Keep receipts in one envelope and record them each evening.
Celebrate small wins, such as a month where savings were fully protected.

blocks.text: Expect the first two or three months to feel awkward. Some lines will be too low and some too high. That is normal. Each month your plan becomes more accurate, and living on it becomes a habit rather than an effort.

takeaways: Set up savings and pots on payday, before spending.
Divide food and transport into weekly amounts.
A 10-minute weekly check catches overspending early.
A planned giving line lets you help others without breaking your budget.

activity.title: Run your first weekly check
steps: At the end of this week, list your budget lines and planned amounts.
Write actual spending next to each from your notes and apps.
Calculate the difference for each line.
Decide how to cover any overspend without touching savings.
Set a reminder on your phone for the same time next week.
activity.evidence: Your planned vs actual table for one week

lessons.title: When plans change: adjusting your budget in hard months
objectives: Revise a budget when income falls or prices rise
Use a priority order to decide what to cut first
Plan ahead for predictable heavy months
Decide when it is reasonable to pause savings and how to restart

blocks.text: No budget survives every month unchanged. Prices of food and fuel can rise quickly, a business can have a slow season, a spouse may lose work, or a family emergency may appear. A good budget is not rigid; it **bends without breaking**. This lesson shows you how to adjust calmly instead of abandoning the plan.
Know your priority order

Decide now, while things are calm, what you will protect first if money becomes tight. A common order is shown below. Your family may differ, but writing it down in advance makes hard decisions faster.

blocks.title: What to protect first
items: Food, shelter, health
Income-earning costs
Minimum debt repayments
Emergency fund saving
Other goals and wants
blocks.caption: When money is tight, cut from the top of this list down, protecting the base.

items: Protect first: food, shelter, essential health, water and safety.
Next: costs that keep income coming, such as transport to work, business stock, phone and data for customers.
Next: minimum repayments on any debts, to avoid penalties and harassment.
Then: a reduced amount to the emergency fund, if at all possible.
Cut first: wants, then non-urgent goals, then non-essential giving.

blocks.name: budget-adjustments
blocks.caption: Adjusting a budget in a hard month is a sign of good management, not failure.

blocks.text: When prices rise

When prices go up, your old food line will not buy the same basket. First, update the budget with real current prices from the market. Then look for substitutes and savings: buying staples in larger quantities with a neighbour, choosing local alternatives to costly items, cooking in larger batches to save gas, and comparing prices between markets. Then reduce wants to make room. Do not ignore the rise and hope; that is how overspending happens.

blocks.title: Worked example: a slow sales month
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells clothes in Onitsha. Her usual planning figure is about ₦150,000 a month, but sales are slow and she expects about ₦110,000 this month. That is a gap of about ₦40,000.
steps: She cuts wants from ₦15,000 to ₦3,000, saving ₦12,000.
She reduces giving from ₦12,000 to ₦5,000, explaining to family that this is a tight month, saving ₦7,000.
She trims food from ₦55,000 to ₦49,000 by cooking in bulk and buying staples with a neighbour, saving ₦6,000.
She reduces her goal savings from ₦20,000 to ₦5,000, saving ₦15,000, but keeps paying rent savings in full.
blocks.result: The revised budget fits ₦110,000 without borrowing. When sales improve, she will restore her goal savings first.

blocks.text: Price rises also affect fixed lines over time. Rent may increase at renewal, school fees may rise at the start of a new session, and transport fares can change when fuel prices move. Ask early: talk to your landlord or the school bursar a few months before the due date, so you can raise your monthly saving in time rather than face a sudden shortfall.
Plan for heavy months you can predict

Some months are always expensive. January often follows festive spending and brings new school term costs. September has school resumption. December has festive costs and travel. Look at your calendar now and mark these months. Then add a small monthly saving line called "heavy months" so the money is ready. This turns a predictable crisis into a planned expense.

head: Heavy month
Typical extra costs
Plan ahead by
rows: School fees, uniforms, books after December spending
Saving monthly for fees; limiting December spending
A small festive savings line all year

blocks.text: When an emergency hits mid-month

If an emergency happens in the middle of the month, follow three steps. First, use the emergency fund for the real cost, not a loan. Second, rewrite the remaining weeks of the budget with the lower amount of money left, cutting wants first. Third, add a rebuild line to next month's budget so the fund recovers. Writing the new plan down, even quickly, stops panic spending and keeps the family on track.
Pausing and restarting savings

In a true crisis, it can be reasonable to pause goal savings for a month or two to protect food and shelter. Try to keep at least a token amount going, even ₦500 a week, so the habit stays alive. Write down the date you will restart. When income recovers, restart savings before restoring wants.

blocks.title: Avoid the borrowing trap
blocks.text: When a month is tight, quick loans from apps or lenders can look like the answer. Borrowing for everyday food and bills, without a clear way to repay, usually makes the next month harder because of interest and fees. Use your emergency fund for real emergencies, adjust the budget, and see Module 4 for how to judge any loan carefully.

takeaways: A good budget bends without breaking.
Write your priority order in advance: food, shelter and income come first.
Update the budget with real prices when costs rise.
Plan monthly for heavy months like January and September.

activity.title: Prepare a hard-month budget
steps: Write your priority order for your household.
Take your current budget and imagine income falls by 25 percent.
Cut and trim lines in your priority order until it balances.
List your heavy months for the next year and their likely extra costs.
Add a monthly "heavy months" savings line to your normal budget.
activity.evidence: Your hard-month budget and list of heavy months

quiz.q: Bola takes home about ₦200,000. Using the classic 50/30/20 guideline, how much goes to savings and extra debt repayment?
Bola's real needs are about ₦150,000 of her ₦200,000. What is the best adjustment?
options: Borrow to keep 30 percent for wants
Use something like 75/5/20 or 75/15/10, keeping a fixed savings share
quiz.explain: Adapt the shares honestly to reality, but protect a savings share by cutting wants.

quiz.q: In what order should you fill a monthly budget?
options: Income, savings, fixed needs, variable needs, giving and wants
quiz.explain: Start with income, pay yourself first, protect needs, then decide giving and wants.

quiz.q: At mid-month, Ese's food line is ₦5,000 over and her wants line is ₦7,000 under. What should she do?
quiz.explain: Moving money from an underspent want covers the overspend without touching savings or borrowing.

quiz.q: Ngozi expects sales to fall by about ₦30,000 this month. What should she cut first?
quiz.explain: Cut from the least important lines first and protect food, shelter and income-earning costs.

quiz.q: Why add a "heavy months" line to a monthly budget?
options: To save gradually for predictable costly months like January and September
quiz.explain: Predictable heavy months become planned expenses when you save for them every month.

modules.title: Building Better Financial Habits
modules.overview: Make good money behaviour last. You will change a costly habit, judge loans by their true cost, protect yourself from loan scams and ponzi schemes, set SMART goals, and pass healthy money habits to the children in your care.

lessons.title: Breaking bad money habits and building good ones
objectives: Identify your own money habits using the cue, routine, reward pattern
Name common habits that drain household money
Replace one bad habit with a better routine
Lend money to others in a way that protects you

blocks.text: Most money problems are not caused by one big decision. They come from small habits repeated many times: a daily snack, a weekly bet, a monthly party outfit, lending without writing anything down. The good news is that habits can be changed, especially when you understand how they work.
How a habit works

Researchers who study behaviour often describe a habit as a loop with three parts. A **cue** is the trigger, such as payday, feeling stressed, seeing a WhatsApp status, or passing a particular shop. A **routine** is what you do, such as buying something. A **reward** is the good feeling you get afterwards. To change a habit, you keep the cue and the reward but swap the routine for a better one.

blocks.title: The habit loop
items: Cue (trigger)
Routine (what you do)
Reward (good feeling)
Repeat until automatic
blocks.caption: Change the routine in the middle and the habit changes, even if the cue stays.

blocks.name: empty-wallet
blocks.alt: A person looking into an empty wallet
blocks.caption: Small repeated habits, not one big purchase, are what usually empty a wallet.

blocks.text: Common habits that drain money

head: Habit
Why it hurts
Better routine
rows: Spending most of the money in the first week after payday
Leaves the last two weeks short, leading to borrowing
Move savings and weekly amounts on payday
The odds are designed so that most players lose over time; losses are often chased with bigger bets
Put the weekly betting amount into savings and track the total
Aso ebi, phones and outings to match friends drain budgets
Use the 30-day wants list and a fixed events budget
Money is often not repaid and relationships suffer
Lend only what you can afford to lose, and write it down
Check balances weekly and turn on alerts

blocks.title: If betting is taking over
blocks.text: If you or someone in your home bets more than planned, borrows to bet, hides betting, or feels unable to stop, treat it as a serious problem. Delete the betting apps, ask the bank to block payments to betting sites if possible, tell a trusted person, and seek support from a counsellor, health worker or faith leader.

blocks.title: Worked example: swapping a routine
blocks.context: For example, Chinwe, a civil servant in Owerri, noticed that every payday she went to the mall with friends and spent heavily. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Cue: payday and a message from friends.
Old routine: shopping at the mall, spending about ₦35,000 each payday.
Reward: feeling good and spending time with friends.
New routine: on payday morning she moves ₦25,000 to savings first, then meets friends for a cheaper outing with a set amount of ₦8,000.
Over 12 months, she saves about ₦300,000 (₦25,000 x 12) and still enjoys time with friends.
blocks.result: Chinwe kept the cue (payday) and the reward (time with friends) but changed the routine. That is why the change lasted.

blocks.text: Lending to family and friends

Helping others is part of our culture, and it is good. But informal lending causes a lot of hidden money stress. Use these rules. Give, rather than lend, when you can afford it and do not expect it back. When you lend, lend only an amount you could survive losing. Write down the amount, date and agreed repayment date, and send a friendly WhatsApp message confirming it so there is a record. Do not lend from your emergency fund or rent savings.

If someone does not repay, decide calmly whether to remind them once, accept the loss, or agree a smaller repayment plan. Do not lend again to someone who has not repaid. Protecting your relationship and your household budget at the same time is easier when the rules are clear from the start.
Building good habits

items: Choose one habit to change, not five at once.
Write down its cue, routine and reward.
Design a new routine that gives a similar reward for less money.
Make the new routine easy: automatic transfers, a list, a set amount of cash.
Track it for 30 days with a tick on a calendar each day you succeed.
Reward yourself for progress, in a way that fits your budget.

blocks.text: Expect slips. If you fall back into an old habit one week, do not give up. Look at what triggered it and plan for that cue next time. Habits take weeks to change, and every week you succeed is money kept.

Your surroundings matter as much as your willpower. Unfollow shopping pages that tempt you, remove saved card details from apps you overspend on, and carry only the cash you plan to use that day. Spend time with friends who support your goals. When a friend asks why you are not joining a costly outing, it is enough to say you are saving for something important.

takeaways: A habit is a loop: cue, routine, reward.
Change the routine and keep a similar reward.
Betting, payday splurges and lending without records are common drains.
Change one habit at a time and track it for 30 days.

activity.title: Change one money habit
steps: Pick one habit that costs you money every week.
Write its cue, routine and reward.
Write a new routine and the money it will save each week.
Mark a calendar for 30 days and tick each successful day.
At the end, add up the money saved.
activity.evidence: Your habit plan and 30-day tick calendar

lessons.title: Borrowing wisely and avoiding loan scams and ponzi schemes
objectives: Work out the true cost of a loan in naira
Tell the difference between borrowing that builds and borrowing that drains
Check a digital lender before using it and know your rights
Spot the signs of loan scams and ponzi schemes

blocks.text: **Debt** is money you borrow and must pay back, usually with extra charges. Borrowing is not always bad. A loan that helps you earn more than it costs can be useful. But debt for everyday spending, or debt you cannot repay, quickly becomes a heavy burden. This lesson helps you judge any loan and protect yourself from fraud.
Borrowing that builds vs borrowing that drains

blocks.title: Two kinds of borrowing
items: Can build
Usually drains
blocks.caption: Ask whether the loan will help you earn or save more than it costs.
left: Stock that sells quickly at profit

blocks.text: Work out the true cost

Before borrowing, ask for three numbers in writing: **how much you receive**, **how much you must pay back in total**, and **by when**. The difference between what you receive and what you repay is the real cost. Some lenders deduct fees upfront, so you receive less than the loan amount but repay the full amount plus interest.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing two loans
blocks.context: For example, Ruth needs about ₦50,000 to buy stock for her provisions shop. These offers are illustrative.
steps: Loan A, a digital lender: she receives ₦50,000 and must repay ₦62,500 in 30 days. Cost: ₦12,500, which is 25 percent for just one month.
Loan B, her registered cooperative: she receives ₦50,000 and repays ₦5,500 a month for 10 months, a total of ₦55,000. Cost: ₦5,000 over 10 months.
She expects the stock to give her about ₦10,000 profit over the month.
With Loan A, the ₦12,500 cost is larger than her ₦10,000 profit, so she loses money.
With Loan B, she pays ₦5,500 a month from profits and still gains.
blocks.result: Ruth chooses Loan B. Comparing the total amount repaid, not just the monthly payment or the speed of approval, showed the real difference.

blocks.text: Digital loan apps: check before you borrow

Loan apps are fast, but some charge very high fees and some have abused borrowers' data. In Nigeria, digital lenders are regulated by the **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)**, which publishes a list of approved lenders on its website. Before borrowing, check that the app is on that list. Read which permissions the app requests. An app that wants access to all your contacts and photos is a warning sign. Shaming borrowers by messaging their contacts is not allowed, and you can report it to the FCCPC.

blocks.name: warning
blocks.alt: A person facing a warning sign
blocks.caption: Pause at every warning sign: a genuine lender never needs your PIN or an upfront fee to a personal account.

blocks.text: Loan scams

items: **Advance fee scams:** someone promises a loan or grant but asks you to pay a "processing", "insurance" or "registration" fee first. Genuine lenders do not ask you to pay to receive a loan into a personal account.
**Fake bank staff:** callers claim to be from your bank and ask for your BVN, card details, PIN or OTP to "approve" a loan or "unblock" your account. Banks never ask for these.
**Fake government grants:** messages on WhatsApp or Facebook promising free government money if you pay a fee or share your details.

blocks.text: Ponzi schemes

A **ponzi scheme** pays earlier members using money from newer members, not from real business profits. It promises high, quick, often guaranteed returns, and it grows by recruitment. It always collapses when new money slows down, and most people, especially those who joined later, lose their money. In Nigeria, MMM Nigeria drew in large numbers of people before it froze members' accounts in December 2016, and many lost their savings.

blocks.title: Ponzi and scam warning signs
blocks.text: Guaranteed high returns. Pressure to act fast. Rewards for recruiting other people. Payment into a personal account. No registration with SEC Nigeria. One of these signs is enough reason to stop and check; several together almost always mean fraud.

Ponzi schemes often look convincing at first. Early members really are paid, and they share screenshots of their profits on WhatsApp and Facebook, which persuades friends and relatives to join. Some schemes use words like "crypto", "forex", "agriculture investment" or "mutual aid" to sound modern or kind. The label does not matter. Ask one question: where does the profit really come from? If nobody can show you a real, checkable business earning that money, keep your savings away.

blocks.title: Protect yourself
blocks.text: Check investment platforms with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Nigeria, lenders with the FCCPC, and banks with the CBN. Never share your PIN, password, OTP or full card details. If you have sent money to a fraudster, contact your bank immediately through its official channels and report to the police.
If you are already in debt

items: List every debt: who you owe, how much, the cost, and the due date.
Stop taking new loans to repay old ones.
Pay at least the minimum on every debt, then put any extra on the most expensive debt first.
Talk to lenders early if you cannot pay; ask for a new repayment plan in writing.
Add a debt repayment line to your budget until it is cleared.

takeaways: Compare loans by the total amount repaid, not the monthly payment.
Borrow only when the loan helps you earn or save more than it costs.
Check loan apps on the FCCPC list and investment platforms with SEC Nigeria.
Guaranteed high returns, recruitment rewards and upfront fees are signs of fraud.

activity.title: Debt and scam check
steps: List any debts you have now with amount, cost and due date.
For one loan you have used or considered, write what you received and what you repaid in total.
Calculate the cost as a naira amount.
Check one loan app or investment offer you have seen against the FCCPC or SEC Nigeria website.
Write the five ponzi warning signs on a card and keep it in your purse.
activity.evidence: Your debt list, one loan cost calculation and your warning-sign card

lessons.title: Setting and reaching financial goals that last
objectives: Write financial goals using the SMART method
Break a big goal into monthly and weekly steps
Track progress and stay motivated
Review your goals every three months

blocks.text: You have now learned to track, save, budget and borrow wisely. Goals bring these skills together and give them direction. A clear goal answers the question: what am I doing all this for? Without goals, saving feels like sacrifice. With goals, every naira saved is a step towards something you truly want.
Write SMART goals
A useful way to write goals is the **SMART** method. Each goal should be:

items: **Specific**: exactly what you want. "Buy a grinding machine for my pepper business", not "grow my business".
**Measurable**: an amount in naira, so you know when you have reached it.
**Achievable**: possible with your current income and budget, even if it takes time.
**Relevant**: important to you and your family, not to impress others.
**Time-bound**: a target date.

blocks.title: From goal to achievement
items: Write SMART goal
Set monthly amount
Save automatically
Check every month
Reach and celebrate
blocks.caption: A goal becomes real when it has a monthly amount and a regular check.

blocks.name: personal-goals
blocks.alt: A woman ticking off personal goals
blocks.caption: Write goals down with amounts and dates, and tick them off as you progress.

blocks.title: Worked example: a SMART business goal
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa makes kunu and zobo in Zaria and sells to schools. She wants to increase production.
steps: Vague goal: "I want to expand my drinks business."
SMART goal: "I will save about ₦180,000 to buy a second large cooking pot, a chest cooler and packaging stock by 30 June, which is 9 months away."
Monthly amount: ₦180,000 divided by 9 is about ₦20,000 a month, or about ₦5,000 a week.
Plan: she saves ₦5,000 every Friday from sales into a locked target savings plan before restocking ingredients.
Progress check: on the last Friday of each month she records the balance on a chart on her wall.
blocks.result: Hauwa can see exactly how close she is each month. If prices rise, she adjusts the target and the weekly amount.

blocks.text: Balance several goals

Most families have more than one goal: an emergency fund, rent, school fees, a business investment, perhaps land or a house in the long term. You cannot fund them all fully at once. A sensible order for many people is: starter emergency fund first, then known upcoming costs like rent and fees, then expensive debt repayment, then business and long-term goals. Give each goal its own pot so progress on one does not hide problems on another.

Notice that the table lists the emergency fund first. Many women want to start with the exciting goal, such as business equipment, but without an emergency fund, the first surprise can force you to raid the business savings or borrow. Building the base first makes every other goal safer. You can still put a small amount towards an exciting goal while the emergency fund grows, so that motivation stays high.

When one goal is reached, do not let the monthly amount disappear into spending. Move it to the next goal on the list. This is sometimes called rolling your savings forward, and it is one of the easiest ways to make steady progress year after year.
Stay motivated

items: Draw a simple progress bar or thermometer and colour it in as you save.
Tell one trusted person about your goal, so they can encourage you.
Celebrate milestones, such as every 25 percent reached, in a small way that fits your budget.
Remember why: keep a picture of the goal, such as the machine or your children's school, on your phone.

blocks.text: Review every three months

Life changes, so goals should be reviewed regularly. Every three months, look at each goal and ask: Is it still important? Is the target amount still correct, given current prices? Am I on track? If not, should I change the monthly amount or the date? Changing a goal is not failure; it is good management. Abandoning goals without reviewing them is what causes problems.

blocks.title: Long-term goals and investing
blocks.text: Some long-term goals, such as retirement, may later involve pensions or investments. Those carry their own risks and rules. Before investing, learn the basics, check that any provider is properly registered (pension fund administrators with PenCom, investment firms with SEC Nigeria), and never invest money you need for your emergency fund.

Goals are personal. A goal that matters to your family will motivate you far more than one copied from a friend or social media. Take time to talk about goals with your spouse or older children, and write them where everyone can see them.

takeaways: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Divide the target by the months available to get a monthly amount.
Give each goal its own pot and fund them in priority order.
Review goals every three months and adjust for price changes.

activity.title: Write your goal plan
steps: Write three financial goals in SMART form.
Calculate the monthly and weekly amount for each.
Put them in priority order.
Draw a progress bar for your top goal.
Set a phone reminder for your three-month review.
activity.evidence: Your SMART goal plan with monthly amounts and a progress bar

lessons.title: Teaching children healthy money habits at every age
objectives: Choose age-appropriate money lessons for your children
Set up a save, spend and share jar system
Use everyday moments, such as market trips, to teach needs vs wants
Model good money behaviour at home

blocks.text: Children learn about money long before anyone teaches them directly. They watch how adults spend, save, argue and give. Teaching children good money habits early is one of the most valuable gifts a parent or guardian can give, and it costs very little. This lesson gives practical ideas for each age group.
What to teach at each age

head: Age
What they can learn
Simple activity
rows: Money is exchanged for things; we wait for things we want
Let them hand money to the seller; use a clear jar for coins and notes
Needs vs wants; saving for a small goal; choices
Give a small regular allowance and three jars: save, spend, share
Budgeting, comparing prices, saving for bigger goals
Let them plan part of the market list with a set amount
Bank accounts, earning, scams, the cost of borrowing
Help them track their own spending and spot online scams

blocks.name: coin
blocks.caption: Even small coins and notes can teach children to save, spend and share wisely.

blocks.text: The three jars

A simple and effective system uses three containers labelled **Save**, **Spend** and **Share**. Whenever a child receives money, from an allowance, gifts or small tasks, they divide it among the jars. The Save jar is for a goal, such as a storybook or football. The Spend jar is for small treats now. The Share jar is for giving, for example at church, at the mosque or to help someone.

blocks.title: Where a child's money goes
items: Money received
Divide into jars
Save for a goal
Spend on small treats
Share with others
blocks.caption: Dividing money as soon as it arrives teaches the habit of paying yourself first.

blocks.title: Worked example: the three jars
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma gives her 8-year-old son Chidi an allowance of about ₦1,000 a week for helping to sweep the compound and wash plates.
steps: They agree: ₦500 to Save, ₦300 to Spend, ₦200 to Share.
Chidi wants a football that costs about ₦5,000.
With ₦500 a week in the Save jar, he will reach ₦5,000 in 10 weeks.
In week 3 he wants to spend his Save money on sweets. Ifeoma reminds him of the football and points to the picture he drew on the jar.
In week 10, he buys the football with his own money.
blocks.result: Chidi learnt to wait, to plan and to feel proud of a goal he reached himself. Those lessons matter more than the amount.

blocks.text: Use everyday moments

items: At the market, ask older children to compare prices of two sizes of the same item and work out which is cheaper per unit.
When a child asks for something, ask: is it a need or a want? Can it wait?
Show them, in simple terms, how you plan the family budget, without sharing worries that frighten them.
Let teenagers see a bank or mobile money statement and explain the charges.

blocks.title: Teach online safety too
blocks.text: Teach children and teenagers never to share PINs, passwords, OTPs or family bank details, never to click links in messages promising free money or gifts, and to tell you if anyone online asks for money or personal information. Explain clearly what a ponzi scheme is, because young people are often targeted on social media.
Allowances, chores and earning

Families differ on whether to give allowances and whether to link them to chores. Some parents pay for extra tasks beyond normal household duties, such as helping in the shop, so children learn that money comes from work. Others give a small fixed amount to practise managing money, and expect normal chores as part of family life. Either way, be consistent, agree the rules clearly and keep the amount small enough for your budget. The habit matters far more than the size.

Older children can also learn from a small business, such as selling sachet drinks during holidays with your supervision. Help them work out costs, price and profit, and decide how much to save from the profit. This connects everything in this course: income, expenses, saving and goals.
Be the example

Children copy what they see. If they see you writing a market list, saving first, saying no to wants politely, and talking calmly about money, they learn that money is something to manage, not fear. Talk openly about saving for school fees and why you sometimes say "not now". Avoid arguments about money in front of them where possible.

If you have older children who earn money from small jobs or a holiday business, help them open a savings account in their name where the bank allows it, with you as guardian. Seeing the balance grow is a strong motivator. Encourage them to set their own SMART goal, just as you learnt in the previous lesson.

Finally, money lessons are not only for your own children. Nieces, nephews and children in your care benefit too. A few minutes a week, repeated over years, can shape how a young person handles money for the rest of their life.

takeaways: Children learn money habits mostly by watching adults.
Match lessons to age, from handing money to a seller to tracking spending.
Save, Spend and Share jars teach planning and generosity.
Teach online and scam safety to older children.

activity.title: Start a money habit with a child
steps: Choose one child in your care and note their age.
Pick one activity from the age table.
If they are 6 or older, label three jars: Save, Spend, Share.
Agree a goal for the Save jar and draw it on the jar.
After four weeks, talk with the child about what they learnt.
activity.evidence: A photo of the labelled jars or a note of the activity and what the child said

quiz.q: Chinwe overspends every payday when friends invite her to the mall. Using the habit loop, what is the best change?
options: Take a loan to keep up
Keep the cue and reward but change the routine: save first, then a cheaper outing with a set amount
quiz.explain: Changing the routine while keeping a similar reward is what makes habit change last.

quiz.q: Loan A gives ₦40,000 and must be repaid as ₦50,000 in one month. What is the cost?
quiz.explain: ₦50,000 repaid minus ₦40,000 received = ₦10,000, which is 25 percent for one month.

quiz.q: Someone on WhatsApp offers a ₦500,000 government grant if Mama Ada first pays a ₦15,000 processing fee. What is this most likely?
quiz.explain: Asking you to pay a fee to receive a loan or grant is a classic advance fee scam.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest sign of a ponzi scheme?
options: A bank savings account with low interest
Guaranteed high monthly returns paid mostly from new members' money and rewards for recruiting
A fixed deposit with a set term
quiz.explain: Ponzi schemes pay old members with new members' money and depend on recruitment, so they collapse.

quiz.q: Before using a loan app in Nigeria, what should she check?
options: That it approves in five minutes
That a friend has used it once
That it appears on the FCCPC list of approved digital lenders and does not demand access to all her contacts
quiz.explain: The FCCPC regulates digital lenders and publishes approved lenders; excessive permissions are a warning sign.

quiz.q: Chidi gets ₦1,000 a week and saves ₦250 of it for a ₦3,000 toy. How many weeks will it take?
quiz.explain: ₦3,000 divided by ₦250 per week = 12 weeks.

quiz.q: Which goal is written in SMART form?
options: I will save about ₦120,000 for a sewing machine by 31 May, saving ₦15,000 a month
I will try to save something
I want to be rich like my neighbour
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and has a date and monthly amount.

finalQuiz.q: Which of the five money decisions does keeping an emergency fund and refusing to share your OTP belong to?
finalQuiz.explain: Protecting the family from shocks and fraud is the protect decision.

finalQuiz.q: Kike wants a new handbag although her current one is fine. Using the 30-day rule, what should she do?
options: Buy it today before the price rises
Take the money from rent savings
Write it on her wants list and decide after 30 days if she can afford it without touching savings
finalQuiz.explain: Delaying wants for 30 days removes impulse buying; many wants disappear on their own.

finalQuiz.q: A tailor's monthly profit over three months was about ₦90,000, ₦60,000 and ₦75,000. What is the safest planning figure?
finalQuiz.explain: The average is ₦75,000 and the lowest ₦60,000; plan between them and save the extra in good months.

finalQuiz.q: School fees are about ₦60,000 per term, three terms a year. How much should be set aside each month?
Which option gives savings both CBN supervision and NDIC deposit insurance up to a limit?
options: A savings account at a licensed bank
finalQuiz.explain: Licensed banks are supervised by the CBN and their deposits are insured by NDIC up to a set limit.

finalQuiz.q: In an ajo, what is the main risk once a member has collected the pot?
options: She may stop contributing, leaving later members short
finalQuiz.explain: Members stopping after collecting is a key failure point; written rules and guarantors help.

finalQuiz.q: Essential monthly expenses are about ₦120,000. What is a reasonable full emergency fund range?
finalQuiz.explain: A common guideline is three to six months of essential expenses.

finalQuiz.q: Take-home pay is about ₦300,000 and needs are about ₦210,000. Which plan keeps a 20 percent savings share?
finalQuiz.explain: 20 percent of ₦300,000 is ₦60,000. With real needs of ₦210,000, wants shrink to ₦30,000.

finalQuiz.q: At a weekly check, transport is ₦4,000 over plan. What is the best response?
options: Move ₦4,000 from an underspent want or trim transport next week
finalQuiz.explain: Fix overspends within the budget, keeping savings and avoiding new debt.

finalQuiz.q: Income falls by a quarter this month. What should be protected first?
options: Food, shelter, health and costs that keep income coming
finalQuiz.explain: Protect the base of the priority pyramid and cut from wants and non-urgent goals first.

finalQuiz.q: A platform promises 40 percent profit every month, guaranteed, and pays a bonus for each friend you bring. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a likely ponzi scheme, check SEC Nigeria registration and stay away
Invest a small amount to test it
Recruit friends quickly before it ends
finalQuiz.explain: Guaranteed high returns plus recruitment rewards are classic ponzi signs.

finalQuiz.q: A 7-year-old receives ₦600 a week. Which system best teaches planning and giving?
options: Divide it into Save, Spend and Share jars with a goal for the Save jar
Keep it for the child without telling them
finalQuiz.explain: The three jars teach paying yourself first, enjoying small treats and generosity.

capstone.title: My Household Money Plan
capstone.brief: Produce a complete household money plan: a money map, one month of tracked spending, a balanced monthly budget, an emergency fund target with a named account, three SMART goals, and a hard-month version of the budget, plus a one-page scam and loan checklist.
steps: Redraw your money map and compare it with the one from Module 1.
Summarise one month of tracked spending by category, marking needs and wants.
Write a balanced monthly budget with savings first and yearly costs as monthly lines.
Set your emergency fund starter and full targets and name where the money is kept, with your licence check.
Write three SMART goals with monthly amounts in priority order.
Prepare a hard-month version of your budget for a 25 percent drop in income.
Write your personal checklist for judging any loan or investment offer.
evidence: Two money maps (start and end of course)
Three SMART goals with monthly amounts
